column1: How do you celebrate Independence Day? Independence Day, for me, is a bit of a mixed bag, a tapestry woven with threads of both patriotic fervor and, dare I say, a touch of skepticism. I find myself, on the Fourth, perpetually torn between the red, white, and blue of national pride and the somber gray of historical reflection. The irony, of course, isn't lost on me: a day ostensibly celebrating freedom often feels curiously constrained by the very traditions it purports to uphold. Fireworks, of course, are a staple, cascading explosions of color against the twilight canvas, mimicking the very battles that birthed this nation. But the cacophony, the sheer volume of sound, inevitably triggers a visceral reaction, a reminder of the din of war and destruction, of the inevitable cost of so-called independence. The Bar-B-Q, the boisterous consumption of grilled meats and sugary sweets, provides a temporary respite, social lubricant, if you will, where people often celebrate with those whose thoughts they may secretly find questionable. Maybe it's also time to move on from that way of thinking.

God is real. Atheists how can you prove me wrong? My challenge to atheists: Do you have the courage of your convictions? If so, buy a Bible and a box of highlighters. Start at the beginning and read every word. Consult yourself. The Bible says you were given the knowledge of good and evil, otherwise you would be immortal. So use what you were given at such an incredibly high price. Highlight every verse you would embrace in your own life, and in the lives of your children. Can a true faith be based on something other than integrity? Be honest about your reservations and doubts. You will soon have a very colorful book! Would you, for example, murder curious Eve for eating an apple, after you had denied her the knowledge of good and evil, meaning she couldn’t know it was evil to sneak a bite? Be honest and ask, has modern science made the concept of God or gods either more or less believable?

What stories in the Bible had the biggest impact on you? The biblical narrative that resonated most with me was the story of the Tower of Babel. It paints a picture of humanity striving for unity and reaching for the heavens, only to be thwarted by a jealous god. It’s a profoundly human tale, brimming with irony and tragic undertones. The idea of a deity threatened by mortal ambition—specifically, the collective human drive for progress—is a fascinating study in insecurity. The audacity of the envisioned structure, the brazen attempt to scale celestial heights that are not the domain of mankind, strikes a chord within me, as it reflects that primal human yearning for transcendence. When you consider the implications of such pride, such striving, such audaciousness, you can grasp the core of the impact. The story’s stark simplicity unveils complex themes of power, control, and the eternal tension between the divine and the mortal. It exposes the inherent flaws in a god who feels threatened enough to disrupt human communication, and it underlines the fundamental human desire for unity, knowledge, and progress. It also highlights the potential pitfalls of unchecked ambition, the ultimate price one pays for violating the boundaries set by the gods. This story, in its brevity, encapsulates the essence of the human condition, and what makes us who we are. It’s a foundational myth, a warning sign of our own potential for hubris, and a testament to the enduring power of human aspirations.

The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The Trinity feels like a theological Frankenstein: a stitched-together construct cobbled from disparate, often contradictory, elements, and forced into a semblance of life. What's the point of this theological contortionism? We’re back to the same exhausted question: why? Why cling to this intellectual absurdity, this metaphysical chimera, when so many other crucial tenets of faith are abandoned with such facile ease? Is the Trinity some sort of bizarre, theological hill they're willing to die on, even as the rest of the landscape crumbles? I'm left wondering if its preservation isn't more about preserving the established order and maintaining a semblance of doctrinal cohesiveness. Perhaps it’s a form of institutional inertia, a reluctance to admit that the emperor, this time, is wearing no clothes—a theological tautology with no substance.

Does the Bible contradict itself? The Bible is a minefield of contradictions, a labyrinth of inconsistencies, a veritable paradox factory. It’s a testament to the erratic nature of its authors, their biases and agendas often clashing like cymbals in a cacophony. Take, for example, the differing accounts of creation in Genesis. We have the initial, grand pronouncements of a singular, all-powerful deity, followed by the more intimate, almost folksy narrative featuring the Garden of Eden and the apple. Then there's the glaring discrepancy present in the Ten Commandments, which contradict the actions of the very god who authored them, a hypocritical deity not worthy of any form reverence or respect. The god of the Bible is, more often than not, a petty tyrant. This is especially evident when one compares the teachings of Jesus, a good man indeed, with the rest of the book.
